title: The Twisted Ladder Inside You
blurb: Four letters, three billion of them, coiled inside almost every cell. How DNA holds the instructions for building a living thing, and how we learned to read them.

blocks.prompt: The Ladder in Every Cell
blocks.text: Your body is made of tiny parts called cells. A cell is so small that you need a microscope to see even one. Curled up inside almost every cell is a long thread called DNA. DNA is shaped like a ladder that has been twisted around and around. The two long sides hold up the rungs in the middle. The rungs are the important part. They spell out instructions, a bit like words on a page. Those instructions tell your cells what to build. Half of your DNA came from your mom. Half came from your dad. That is why you look a little like both of them.

blocks.prompt: The Twisted Ladder in Every Cell
blocks.text: Almost every cell in your body carries a full set of instructions for building you. Those instructions are written in DNA. If you could pull a strand of DNA straight, it would look like a ladder. Two long rails run up the sides. Between them sit the rungs. Then the whole ladder twists, like a rope ladder someone spun around. Scientists call that shape a double helix. The instructions are written with only four letters: A, T, G, and C. Each letter is a chemical, and each rung of the ladder is made of two letters holding hands. The pairing never changes. A always joins with T. G always joins with C. That simple rule is what makes DNA so useful. If you know one side of the ladder, you can work out the other side every time. Your cells use that rule when they copy themselves. The ladder unzips down the middle. Each half then builds a new partner, letter by letter, until there are two complete ladders where there was one. Your body does this billions of times a day, and it almost never makes a mistake.

blocks.prompt: Four Letters, Three Billion Long
blocks.text: Stretch out the DNA from a single one of your cells and it would run about six feet, longer than most adults are tall. Now consider that it is packed inside a cell you cannot see without a microscope. To fit, the strand winds around tiny protein spools, coils, and coils again, until it forms the compact bundles we call chromosomes. You have 46 of them in almost every cell, arranged in 23 pairs. What is written on all that thread? A message, spelled with an alphabet of four chemical letters: A, T, G, and C. Your copy runs to roughly three billion pairs of letters. Stretches of that message are called genes, and each gene is a set of directions for building one protein. Proteins do the actual work of a body. They digest your lunch, carry oxygen in your blood, and build the lens of your eye. Humans have around 20,000 protein-coding genes, which is fewer than scientists expected when they started counting. The four-letter alphabet is not unique to you. It is the same alphabet used by oak trees, by mushrooms, by the bacteria in a puddle. Only the message differs. That is a clue about the deep past. Every living thing we have ever examined runs on the same code, which suggests they all inherited it from a shared ancestor that lived billions of years ago. And the message is nearly identical between people. Compare your DNA to a stranger's on the other side of the world and about 99.9 percent of it matches. Everything that makes you look and sound like yourself is written in the remaining tenth of a percent.

blocks.prompt: The Photograph That Cracked the Code
blocks.text: By 1952, biologists agreed that DNA carried heredity. What nobody could explain was how. A molecule that stores instructions must do two jobs at once: hold a message, and copy that message perfectly. No one had seen a shape that could manage both. At King's College London, Rosalind Franklin was working on the shape. Her method was X-ray crystallography: fire X-rays at a fiber of DNA and photograph the pattern they scatter into. The molecule itself stays invisible. What you get is a smudged arrangement of spots, and from that pattern you calculate backward to the structure. It is a demanding kind of detective work, and Franklin was exceptionally good at it. In May 1952, she and her student Raymond Gosling produced an image now known as Photo 51. Its blurred X of spots was the signature of a helix, and the spacing carried the measurements. Franklin was still working carefully through her calculations when Maurice Wilkins, a colleague, showed Photo 51 to James Watson without her knowledge. Watson and Francis Crick, at Cambridge, had been building models out of cardboard and wire. The photograph, along with unpublished data of Franklin's that reached them through a report, gave them what they lacked. In 1953 they published the answer: two strands winding around each other in opposite directions, sugar and phosphate on the outside, the four bases paired in the middle, A with T and G with C. The pairing rule solved both problems in one stroke. It explained the message, and it explained the copying, because an unzipped strand dictates its own replacement. Watson and Crick noted the point in a famously restrained sentence, observing that the pairing they had proposed immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin was not named. She had died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37, and the prize is not awarded after death. Whether she would have been included had she lived is a question the people involved answered differently for the rest of their lives.

6.title: The Twisted Ladder Inside You
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Structure published in 1953
The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003
The last gaps were not closed until 2022
Sequencing fell from billions of dollars to hundreds
CRISPR began as a bacterial defense against viruses
First CRISPR therapy approved in 2023

blocks.prompt: Three Billion Letters and the Right to Read Them
blocks.text: Ask what DNA is and you get a tidy answer: a molecule shaped like a twisted ladder, its rungs built from four bases, A, T, G, and C, paired by a rule that never varies. A with T. G with C. That answer is correct, and it is also the least interesting thing about DNA. The interesting part is what the rule made possible. Because the pairing is rigid, each strand of the ladder contains the full information of the other. Unzip the molecule and you do not destroy the message. You produce two copies of it. Watson and Crick saw this the moment they had the structure and said so, in one of the most understated sentences in science, noting that the pairing they had postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material. Heredity, which had been a mystery for as long as people had noticed that children resemble their parents, turned out to be a consequence of geometry. For fifty years after 1953, reading a genome was brutally slow. Sequencing meant working out the order of the letters, and early methods produced them a few hundred at a time. The Human Genome Project set out in 1990 to read all three billion pairs in a single human genome. It took thirteen years and roughly three billion dollars, and even then it left gaps in the hardest, most repetitive stretches. Those final gaps were not closed until 2022. Then the price collapsed. A human genome that cost billions in 2003 can now be sequenced for a few hundred dollars in a day or two. Nothing about the biology changed. The machines changed, and a rate of improvement that outran even the semiconductor industry turned an epic national project into a routine order. Cheap reading produced an obvious next question. If we can read the message, can we edit it? In 2012, researchers described how a bacterial defense system called CRISPR could be aimed at any chosen sequence of DNA and made to cut it, letting the cell's own repair machinery rewrite what was there. Bacteria had been using the system to shred invading viruses for a very long time. Turned into a tool, it made editing a gene something a well-equipped lab could attempt in an afternoon. In 2023, regulators approved the first CRISPR-based therapy for patients, a treatment for sickle cell disease that corrects the problem in a patient's own blood cells. So here is where the tidy molecule leaves us. We can read a person's genome quickly and cheaply, and we can increasingly rewrite it. Both abilities cut in more than one direction. A genome predicts some things about a person's health, which is precisely why an insurer, an employer, or a police department might want to see it, and why a genome donated to a testing company is not only the donor's information. Your close relatives are written in your sample too, and they never consented. Editing raises the sharper version of the question. Repairing a gene that causes a painful disease in a living patient is hard to argue against. Editing an embryo, whose changes would pass to every descendant, is a different act, and in 2018 a Chinese scientist did it anyway, to widespread condemnation and a prison sentence. None of these questions are biological. The chemistry is settled and it is not complicated. The four letters pair the same way in a laboratory in Shenzhen, in a bacterium in a hot spring, and in the cells reading this page. What is unsettled is who decides what gets read, what gets written, and on whose behalf. That decision has never belonged to the molecule.
